sources.title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited (transcript)
sources.note: Read to the end of the file, but the transcript is truncated mid-sentence at about 01:08:30 of the recording, so the closing minutes are missing. Mostly Kevin Gregory (guest/producer) demoing; Dex cards only where he adopts or generalises.

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you give the model a way to fix its own mistakes
cards.claim: Backpressure is any automated feedback loop (tests, compiler, type check, browser screenshot via MCP) that lets the model correct itself so the human only reviews what matters.
cards.evidence_detail: Definition given in answer to a chat question; no numbers.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md Commands section / phase routine: name the exact self-check commands per phase

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you cannot accidentally steer a type checker
cards.claim: Good backpressure is deterministic, because an LLM judge can be steered to either praise or condemn the same code depending on how it is asked.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument by example (same model asked 'is this great' vs 'what is wrong' gives opposite verdicts); no measurement.
cards.landing: Verifier design: prefer scripted checks over LLM refuters where a deterministic check exists

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: LLM as judge is useful in certain cases, but I think it's often over applied
cards.claim: A builder agent plus a manager agent on the same model adds little over folding the manager's instructions into the builder prompt; LLM-as-judge is over-applied.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion in reply to a chat question about LLM as judge.
cards.landing: Reviewer/refuter agents: question whether an extra same-model pass beats a better builder prompt or a script

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can do a reviewer agent to like, and we do this in our PR flows
cards.claim: A reviewer agent that compares the plan with what was implemented and lists deviations is still useful, because the implementer almost always adds something between phases and the plan should document it.
cards.evidence_detail: Says it almost always finds an added item between two phases; no counts.
cards.landing: Per-PR Opus reviewer: add an explicit 'deviations from Plan @ sha' section

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a global stop hook where it's like whenever the agent thinks it's done talking
cards.claim: The most deterministic backpressure is a global stop hook that runs the checks whenever the agent thinks it is done and injects any failure back into context.
cards.evidence_detail: Offered as the strongest of three options (prompt it, document it in AGENTS.md, stop hook); not measured.
cards.landing: Hooks (a harness review SKIPPED hooks; this re-opens it): Stop hook running lint/typecheck/tests

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The back pressure mechanism doesn't have to be binary. It just needs to be observable.
cards.claim: Backpressure need not be pass/fail; it only needs to return tokens (CLI output, stdout) that tell the model what went wrong.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated by Vaibhav; Dex agrees ('the model has to be able to get tokens in to tell it what was wrong'). Dex adoption only.
cards.landing: Verifier output format: make check scripts print actionable text, not just exit codes

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: make that an auto, figure out a way to run a test
cards.claim: When reviewing plans, convert 'manually curl the running service' verification steps into automated tests that spin up the service on its own port, so the plan's verification is machine-runnable.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes his own plan-review habit; the RPI plan structure exists so the model is told exactly what to run.
cards.landing: Phase plan template: every acceptance step must be an automated command; manual steps flagged

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: spend three days designing the back pressure system, not even writing the code
cards.claim: The best AI engineers he saw spent days designing the checks (test cases in plain text) and then ran Opus in a loop for two days to get about 20,000 lines of working code with no human in the loop.
cards.evidence_detail: Second-hand observation of other engineers from around May/June 2025; '20,000 lines' and 'two days' are approximate, unattributed.
cards.landing: Phase 0 of each ship-plan phase: write the verification list before the implementation brief

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: we'll actually build what I call a learning test
cards.claim: For any black-box dependency (closed API, binary, SDK flags), write a small runnable test that proves how it behaves instead of trusting docs or model weights, and do it as part of research.
cards.evidence_detail: Claude Agent SDK example: assumed allowedTools was a whitelist, found otherwise only after deep implementation; also cites OpenAI responses API thinking-token behaviour.
cards.landing: Phase routine research step; fits the knowledge-store pilot (verified diagnoses) and cold-resume facts

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The assumption lands in the research ... makes it into the plan. That makes it into our implementation.
cards.claim: A wrong assumption from docs or model weights propagates through research, plan and implementation, and is discovered in a late phase, forcing a redo of everything; vet assumptions early where leverage is highest.
cards.evidence_detail: Argued from experience; ties back to his 'advanced context engineering' leverage point.
cards.landing: Plan review gate: list assumptions about external systems and the evidence for each before phase 1

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We have probably a hundred of these now
cards.claim: Keep learning tests as a documented contract with external systems you do not control and re-run them manually (not every CI run) on dependency upgrades to see which contract broke.
cards.evidence_detail: Says his team has roughly a hundred; example: Claude SDK session resume used to give a new id, later changed, and SDK v1 to v2 changed fork behaviour.
cards.landing: A saved, re-runnable contract-check workflow for Expo/Railway/Supabase/R2 behaviours; CLAUDE.md 'build traps' could point at them

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: read the V2 docs and the existing learning tests and create a learning test
cards.claim: Having a few existing learning tests as examples lets a coding agent write a new one from the docs in one prompt, run it, and rewrite its own 'key findings' header from the real output.
cards.evidence_detail: Live demo: 7 tests written, all passed first run, agent then updated findings and found an error-timing quirk.
cards.landing: A skill (.claude/skills) for 'write a learning test'; findings header feeds the knowledge store

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: EVALs are a form of learning tests.
cards.claim: Evals and playground experiments are learning tests for an LLM dependency: poke it to see how it behaves before wiring it into code, and run them manually rather than on every CI loop.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated in dialogue; no numbers.
cards.landing: Verifier tuning: run eval-style checks on demand, not per commit

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you don't have to read the code to see that a boundary was broken
cards.claim: Human-facing backpressure: auto-generate a dependency diagram of the codebase so a human can see a broken module boundary without reading code (a Vaibhav tool Dex frames as backpressure for the human).
cards.evidence_detail: BAML team's generated dependency matrix caught a bad import (bridge depending on compiler); Dex frames and endorses it.
cards.landing: Call-graph/boundary tooling (SKIPPED by harness review); relates to import-linter contracts already in CI

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: You should put in a hook that makes it so that it can't edit that file.
cards.claim: Dex proposes a hook that blocks the agent from editing a load-bearing boundary-config file; Vaibhav counters that it sometimes must change and a required human code review or PR rule on that file is better.
cards.evidence_detail: Brief exchange; resolved toward a review rule rather than a hard block.
cards.landing: Protected-paths rule (CODEOWNERS or PreToolUse hook) for import-linter config, alembic head, CLAUDE.md invariants

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you don't generally want to automate the checking of this file
cards.claim: Spend human review on the few high-leverage files whose errors let hundreds of wrong decisions leak into the codebase, and check them two ways (read plus a visual).
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoning from the boundary-file example; 'two-pass accounting' analogy.
cards.landing: Owner view: a short list of 'human must read' files per PR

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: invest time in tooling
cards.claim: Investing in pretty-printers and test frameworks for tool output (so the model sees a prettified response rather than raw JSON) is itself backpressure infrastructure worth building.
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's closing point citing Dex's learning-test harness for the Claude CLI; Dex does not dispute.
cards.landing: Check-script output design; context cost of verifier output

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: sometimes you should do what feels like too much
cards.claim: Learn the right amount of planning per problem by deliberately overshooting in both directions (vibe the small things, over-plan others) and binary-searching toward the right range; the range shifts with models and problems.
cards.evidence_detail: Analogy to executive coaching; no data.
cards.landing: Phase sizing and routine weight: allow a lighter routine for small phases

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you give guidelines. You say, hey, for 80 % of people, we should always do the same process
cards.claim: Vaibhav argues a fixed process puts most people in the good zone and Dex agrees by encouraging try-small-then-plan instincts; a default process helps when people lack bandwidth to explore.
cards.evidence_detail: Mostly Vaibhav; Dex endorses and adds the 'if it feels too small, skip planning' heuristic.
cards.landing: Phase routine as a default with a documented skip rule for tiny changes

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Codex 5.3, go try to solve this, like just based on the ticket
cards.claim: Run competing attempts in parallel (an Opus plan/design session alongside a Codex 5.3 attempt straight from the ticket) to learn the solution space; Vaibhav runs one-shot vs planned in two repos.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal practice; Codex 5.3 described as slow but liked.
cards.landing: Workflow library: optional 'two strategies' exploration for hard phases

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: how do we optimize for a really fast feedback loop
cards.claim: For things AI is bad at judging (UI, components) where a human is still required, optimise for a fast human feedback loop with tools like Storybook; planned as a follow-up episode.
cards.evidence_detail: Announced scope in the intro and mentioned again near the end; not demonstrated.
cards.landing: Web manager UI phases: component-level visual check instead of full-app click-through

cards.source_title: AI That Works #44 Agentic Backpressure Deep Dive
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Michael Feathers ... working effectively with legacy code
cards.claim: Learning tests come from legacy-code practice (poke the system from outside); the term has poor SEO and is also called proof-based development.
cards.evidence_detail: Attribution only; provenance, not an adopted mechanism.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: define what are the boundaries outside of your agentic sphere that you want human approval
cards.claim: Define the actions that leave the sandbox (public posts, mass emails) as approval-required one-way doors, and let anything editable later run automatically.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex generalises Kevin's pipeline design and says it was the entire thesis behind HumanLayer.
cards.landing: Owner approval gates in the phase routine (deploy, migration, customer messaging)

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: worth reviewing it every time, rather than trying to automate it to 99.9 % quality
cards.claim: If the AI gets a post right about 90% of the time, keep reviewing every one rather than chase near-perfect automated quality.
cards.evidence_detail: Weekly production went from 3-4 hours to about an hour (web app era), then to about 10 minutes with Kevin's commands (Kevin's figure).
cards.landing: Reviewer effort policy; owner view stays human

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: make a prompt that is everything you have to do you can always leave in like stop
cards.claim: Write the whole process as one prompt/command with explicit 'stop and get the human to do this part' steps, then replace stops with automations one at a time.
cards.evidence_detail: Says he does this for monthly investor updates and weekly sales reports, half automated; links to skills.
cards.landing: Phase routine as a slash command or skill with human-stop markers, filled in incrementally

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: top level model is just orchestrating all of these tools that under the hood are doing their own AI
cards.claim: Use a cheap tool-calling model (Sonnet 4.5) as top-level orchestrator of CLIs that each do their own focused LLM call in a separate context window; Sonnet is great at tool calling but does not think much.
cards.evidence_detail: Kevin runs the whole pipeline on Sonnet 4.5 to save tokens; Dex remarks this matches what good AI engineers say.
cards.landing: Effort/model routing: orchestrator on a cheaper model, hard steps behind scripts or sub-calls

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the thing that the agent learns while it's working ... now let's bake that into a deterministic code
cards.claim: Let an agent discover a workflow once (screenshot-and-click), then have it write the result as deterministic automation code so AI is no longer needed to rediscover the page.
cards.evidence_detail: Kevin's Riverside browser automation; Dex states the principle; caveat from Kevin: watch the browser live, the agent looped on a popup.
cards.landing: Saved workflows: crystallise recurring agent procedures into scripts (Workflow library)

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: take the output and then do a different structure generation on it to find all the things that are wrong
cards.claim: A generate, then critique-into-structured-list, then rewrite-with-input-plus-critique pipeline (plus a final structure-preservation pass) is the pattern he likes for removing AI-slop; Kevin still needs one or two human edit rounds.
cards.evidence_detail: Kevin reports 4-6 edit rounds before, 1-2 after; Dex reacts to the live run and prefers the output.
cards.landing: Reviewer design: separate 'list defects' pass from 'fix' pass; relevant to refute-by-default

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude doesn't have a PTY, so you can't actually go back and forth with it.
cards.claim: Claude Code cannot be paused for interactive breakpoints, so to debug a step in a pipeline run the underlying CLI yourself.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated while Kevin tried breakpoints inside a Claude Code run; Kevin then ran the CLI directly.
cards.landing: Workflow scripts: keep each step runnable as a standalone script for debugging

cards.source_title: AI That Works #45 AI Content Pipeline Revisited
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude Code ... robustness and flexibility and almost like squishiness over a set of deterministic tools
cards.claim: Claude Code as the top-level orchestrator adds tolerance over deterministic tools (Kevin's command instructions were stale after a rename and it still worked), which makes imperfect written procedures workable.
cards.evidence_detail: Kevin observed stale instructions being worked around; Dex frames it as a general pattern.
cards.landing: Phase routine robustness: stale step names tolerated but should be fixed; doc-drift check

cards.source_title: AI That Works #43 Prompting Is Becoming a Product Surface
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: this is your deterministic overlay that the engineers maintain
cards.claim: Engineering keeps a fixed deterministic layer (house rules such as short list items) on top of user-controlled prompt fragments, so non-technical users can steer output without owning the root prompt.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex restates Vaibhav's BAML dynamic-schema design; product-side, not coding-agent.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (product UX for customer-facing text)

cards.source_title: AI That Works #43 Prompting Is Becoming a Product Surface
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: playing the back and forth between unstructured and structured
cards.claim: Dex says he is high-conviction that the hard problem is UX for multi-step pipelines that move between unstructured and structured forms while staying digestible to non-technical users (a cursor-style chat plus red/green diff UI).
cards.evidence_detail: Conviction statement, no evidence.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

gaps: The 2026-02-17 transcript is truncated mid-sentence at about 01:08:30; the closing key-takeaways section is missing.
For the 2026-02-03 episode I read Dex's own turns (about 30) in full plus README and meta, and only skimmed Vaibhav's turns; any Dex ideas that sit inside Vaibhav's long turns are unseen.
EPISODE.md for #44 is a repo write-up of unclear authorship; it was not carded.
Several chat-question answers in #44 (whiteboard images, the Geoffrey Huntley backpressure post) were not viewable; images were not read.
No prior 'dumb zone', context-window or compaction material appears in these three episodes, so L2 evidence is thin.
Auto-caption errors: 'Cargosto' is probably 'cargo-stow' or similar, 'Nistan' name uncertain; not quoted.
